deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two unrelated groups of notes. A: holomorphic solutions of a linear ODE near a point where the leading coefficient vanishes. B: periods of abelian integrals on a Riemann surface and the normalisation that leads to theta functions.

A. Linear ODE at a singular point.
(1) Riemann starts from a0(x) y^(n) + a1(x) y^(n-1) + ... + a_n(x) y = 0. Superscripts y^n, y^{n-1} on the page mean derivatives y^(n), y^(n-1).
(2) He considers a point x = α where a0(α) = 0. There the equation cannot be solved for y^(n).
(3) He differentiates once: a0 y^(n+1) + (a0'+a1) y^(n) + (a1'+a2) y^(n-1) + ... + (a_{n-1}'+a_n) y' + a_n' y = 0.
(4) He starts the second derivative: a0 y^(n+2) + (2a0'+a1) y^(n+1) + ... The coefficient 2a0'+a1 comes from a0' + (a0'+a1).
(5) At x = α, where a0 = 0, the original equation becomes a constraint among the lower derivatives: a1 y^(n-1) + a2 y^(n-2) + ... + a_n y = 0.
(6) The differentiated equation at α reads (a0'+a1) y^(n) + Σ_k (a_k'+a_{k+1}) y^(n-k) = 0, with a_{n+1} := 0 (my notation).
(7) Riemann writes (a1'+a2)/a1 = (a2'+a3)/a2 = ... = a_n'/a_n. This says the tail of the differentiated equation is proportional to the constraint in (5). If so, the tail vanishes on solutions and the relation degenerates to (a0'+a1) y^(n) = 0. The degree of freedom in the initial data then changes (y^(n) is forced to 0, or is free if a0'+a1 = 0) (my interpretation).
(8) The scattered lists of derivatives (y^n, y^{n-1}, y^{n+p}, y^{n-2}, some underlined, one row struck out) look like bookkeeping. They record which derivatives at α are determined by which differentiated equation. This is an early version of counting the free initial data, i.e. the holomorphic solutions, at a singular point.

B. Abelian integrals.
(9) The sketch top left shows a cut with banks labelled w' and w''. The label w'' - w' is the jump of the integral across the cut, constant along it: the period / modulus of periodicity.
(10) The large drawing shows a surface, a sphere labelled s^2 (possibly s^2 of an algebraic equation F(s,z) = 0), and nested closed curves with slits, i.e. cross-cuts. With 'k1+k2' and 'k1'+k2'' alongside, it illustrates how periods add when cuts are combined.
(11) He considers the general integral of the first kind α1 w1 + α2 w2 + ... + αp wp + const.
(12) Two integrals w, w' have periods k1..kp, l1..lp and k1'..kp', l1'..lp' along the two systems of cross-cuts.
(13) Riemann's bilinear period relation: Σ_α (k_α l_α' - k_α' l_α) = 0 (underlined).
(14) The diagonal matrix with πi on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere is Riemann's normalisation: the A-periods of the normalised integrals w_μ are πi δ_{μν}. The B-periods are then a_{μ,ν}.
(15) Applying (13) to w_μ, w_ν gives πi a_{νμ} - πi a_{μν} = 0. This is the symmetry a_{μ,ν} = a_{ν,μ} written on the page, needed for the theta function ϑ(...) noted there.
(16) At the bottom, √x, √(1-x) (?) and √(1-x^2) are simple algebraic functions used as examples of branching and cuts. A disc crossed by chords is another cut-system sketch.

This matches the content of Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen (1857), §§ on the normalisation of the periods and the theta series.
errors: No algebraic errors. The differentiated equation and the coefficient 2a0'+a1 of the second derivative are correct.
The chain of ratio equalities in (7) is stated without its purpose or its domain of validity. It is only meaningful at x = α, and it divides by a_k, which may vanish. Its role has to be inferred.
The bilinear relation is written without the normalising 1/(πi) or orientation conventions. As a relation between two integrals of the first kind it is correct as written (= 0).

results.what: Differentiating a linear ODE to obtain conditions on derivatives at a point where the leading coefficient vanishes (determining which initial data are free)
results.modern_name: Local analysis at a singular point of a linear ODE (precursor of Frobenius/Fuchs indicial analysis)
results.usually_credited_to: Fuchs (1866), Frobenius (1873); Riemann's P-function work (1857) treats the second-order case

results.what: Σ (k_α l'_α − k'_α l_α) = 0 for two abelian integrals of the first kind
Normalisation of A-periods to πi δ_{μν}; symmetry a_{μν} = a_{νμ} of the B-period matrix; use in theta function ϑ
results.modern_name: Normalised period matrix and its symmetry (Riemann theta function)

results.what: Jump w'' − w' of an integral across a cross-cut, constant along the cut

deep.surprise_reason: The bilinear relations, the πi normalisation and the symmetric period matrix are Riemann's own published results (1857), and he lectured on them in 1855–56. This page is a working sketch. A dating near 1853 would be a minor point of chronology, not a new attribution. The ODE part is elementary.

checkable.asserts: Differentiated ODE coefficients (a_{k-1}'+a_k) are correct (n=3 case)
Coefficient of y^(n+1) in the second derivative is 2a0'+a1 (n=3 case)
The bilinear relation applied to normalised integrals w_mu, w_nu (A-periods πi δ) gives symmetry a_{mu,nu}=a_{nu,mu}

transcription_corrections: Superscripts y^n, y^{n-1}, y^{n+1}, y^{n+2}, y^{n+p} denote derivatives y^(n) etc., not powers.
The struck-out row '[-y^{n-1} y^{n-3}-]' is crossed through by a stroke under the main ODE line.
'ϑ(ϑ̊², z)' is unclear. It is probably ϑ with arguments relating to the period quantities; the reading is uncertain.
The top-left item '∂²w/∂θ' is uncertain. It may be ∂w/∂θ or ∂²w/∂θ² (Laplacian-type notation); it is preceded by a struck-out word.
The scribble near the top is 'w''−w'' (jump across a cut), with w'' and w' labelling the two banks of a drawn cut.
The bottom roots read √x, √(1−x) (struck through/overwritten), y_1, √(1−x²).
